I've often wondered this myself, but I think it was more than just powerhouse graphics that stole the show. The entire home experience was what gamers started to prefer. Being at home, sitting on the comfy couch, snacks within an arm's reach, the pause button, friends looking on (or playing along), etc. are all things you can't duplicate in an arcade with the exception of a few of those, but of course at a cost.

The games have also changed too. Arcade games were built to have quick, fast levels so that they can take as many quarters as possible from you in the shortest amount of time. Then they had to balance that with repeat gameplay or versus games where you'd want to play with someone to compete. This is why fighting and racing games were all the rage back in those days (at least in the 90s arcades). The home gaming experience is slow and progressive with huge epic adventures being the favorite type of game now.

Of course online, you still have some favorite multiplayers like first person shooters, but again, playing online with 20 different people while you enjoy the comfort of your own home is more exciting than holding on to a dirty joystick and playing with a couple people in an arcade. Also, arcades can be intimidating. I remember as a kid wanting to play Mortal Kombat all the time, but sometimes you'd see that older kid that never lost and you never wanted to waste your money. Playing games at home eliminates that intimidation...and saves you money!

Don't get me wrong, I'm with you as far as wishing for the old days to come back, but I fear that arcades are now relegated to the backrooms of bars and/or multi entertainment venues such as Dave & Busters.

In some countries (i.e. Japan) arcades are thriving, but as far as the American markets go I think they are dead, with a few exceptions. There are just so many ways to game these days, and for much cheaper. When I was a kid, and I bought consoles, I was always looking for the arcade experience because their machines were superior. But now they're not, plain, and simple. Everything I want can be done at home.

I think bringing them back here in the US will be tough. The arcades used to be so much better than anything available in the home. When you talk about a game being better, most people in the US tend to think of graphics. Well, home is just as good as arcades on that front now. For arcades to come back, there is going to have to be a very strong mix of experiences that cannot be replicated at home. For that reason I think the comeback will be tough.

In Japan, where arcades never died, they have evolved to to experiences, but in the US, they died off, now to stock an arcade with new machines (like what is in Japan, not just classics) would cost so much and the risk would be extremely high, as most people would think, I can play better looking games at home, and not even walk in the door.

Japan never had to educate consumers about what an arcade is about, because they constantly evolved and stayed ahead of home consoles. Here re-education would be needed, that the arcade is a social place, and not just about graphics but offering things that you couldn't otherwise do at home. Because of the cost of educating potential customers would be so high, and the cost of buying modern arcades would be so high, I very highly doubt we will ever see them come back in the US. I wish it would happen, but not likely. Best bet may be for some of the "beer cades" to slowly bring in some of these modern games from Japan, and people would start to realize what a modern arcade could be, but I wouldn't bet on it happening. Sad state of things.

Forgive me for replying to a sort of old-ish post, but I just recently visited a Dave & Busters for a niece's party, and I was absolutely heartbroken. The visit was enough to convince me that arcades are dead here in the states. The whole place was filled with giant arcade cabinet versions of mobile games, like Angry Birds, and a handful of poorly-calibrated, aging shooters. Not one fighting game. No bullet hell games No pinball machines. The only thing that even had a joystick on it, aside from a pair of flight sim games, was the OMG SO RETRO giant Pac-Man game. They didn't even have a Golden Tee by the bar. To add insult to injury, each game costs a different, asymmetrical amount of credits to play, like 6.5 credits, so you're going to be stuck with remainders of money on the card when it's empty. The final kick in the dick was playing one level of a Star Wars Battle Pod, surviving, and then being told I had to pay more to continue. It was a really disheartening, nickel-and-diming-to-death experience, and I will never set foot in a D&B again.
